passages.t: The bronze altar, the Sea, and the basins
passages.happening:
‘He made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high’ (verse 1). ‘He also made the Sea of cast metal. It was circular in shape, measuring ten cubits from rim to rim, five cubits in height, and thirty cubits in circumference’ (verse 2). It rests on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each direction (verse 4). ‘It was a handbreadth thick, and its rim was fashioned like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It could hold three thousand baths’ (verse 5).

‘He also made ten basins for washing and placed five on the south side and five on the north. The parts of the burnt offering were rinsed in them, but the priests used the Sea for washing’ (verse 6). Ten gold lampstands, ten tables and a hundred gold bowls are made for the sanctuary, and the courtyards are built (verses 7-10).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 built the house; this chapter fills it, moving from the bronze objects in the courtyard, where the people gathered and sacrifices were offered, to the gold furnishings inside. The bronze altar, which Kings mentions only in passing, was about thirty feet square and fifteen high, far larger than the tabernacle's, and must have been approached by steps or a ramp.

Water mattered because approaching a holy God required cleanness. The tabernacle had one bronze basin, kiyyor, for the priests' hands and feet; the temple multiplied it into the great Sea and ten basins. A bath was a liquid measure often estimated at around 22 liters, about six gallons, though estimates vary.

The name Sea, yam, may carry a meaning. In the stories of Israel's neighbors the sea was a power of chaos, and in Canaanite texts from Ugarit, Sea is a god defeated by Baal. In Israel's temple the sea is a bronze basin made by human hands, resting on oxen and serving God's priests. Many see a quiet claim that the LORD rules the waters, though the text does not spell it out.

Verse 2 gives a diameter of ten cubits and a circumference of thirty, a ratio of exactly three, and skeptics have sometimes called this an error. Most answer that the figures are round, as ancient measures were, and that the rim was a handbreadth thick and flared like a lily, so the diameter may have been taken across the outer rim and the circumference around the body below it. It is a builder's description, not geometry. First Kings 7:26 gives the Sea two thousand baths, and verse 5 here three thousand. Suggestions include a copying error, different sizes of the bath measure in different periods, or one figure for what it usually held and the other for its full capacity. The difference is real, and no explanation has won general agreement.
passages.later: The tabernacle's basin was the one ‘with which Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and feet’ (Exodus 30:19). A psalm says, ‘The floodwaters have risen, O LORD; the rivers have raised their voice; the seas lift up their pounding waves’ (Psalm 93:3), and then that above the roar of many waters the LORD on high is majestic.
passages.asks: The priests could not serve until they had washed. Ask what in you needs cleansing before you come near God. And ask whether you believe he has made a way for that cleansing.

passages.happening:
‘So Huram finished the work that he had undertaken for King Solomon in the house of God’ (verse 11): the pillars, the capitals, the pomegranates, the stands, the basins, the Sea and its oxen, ‘All these objects that Huram-abi made for King Solomon for the house of the LORD were of polished bronze’ (verse 16). ‘The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan between Succoth and Zeredah’ (verse 17), so much bronze that its weight could not be determined (verse 18).

Solomon also makes the gold furnishings: the golden altar, the tables for the Bread of the Presence, the lampstands and their lamps, the snuffers, bowls, ladles and censers, ‘and the gold doors of the temple’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a catalog, and its form is part of its meaning. It moves from the courtyard to the sanctuary, from bronze to gold, from the common to the most holy. The verb he made comes thirteen times. Phrases such as as prescribed and according to their specifications tie the temple to the law of Moses: it is a faithful enlargement of the tabernacle pattern, not something new. The one lampstand, menorah, of the tabernacle became ten. The Bread of the Presence, literally bread of the face, was set before the LORD and replaced every Sabbath.

Casting in the Jordan Valley made sense: its clay soils suited large metal casting, and archaeologists have found signs of ancient metalworking in the region. Kings names Zarethan where Chronicles names Zeredah. Casting a basin the size of the Sea in one piece was a major achievement for the time.

For the Chronicler's readers this list was a memory. Their second temple lacked much of this splendor. Solomon's bronze had been broken up and carried to Babylon. The catalog told them what had been and what worship was meant to be.
passages.later: Second Kings remembers the end of this bronze: ‘the Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars and stands and the bronze Sea in the house of the LORD, and they carried the bronze to Babylon’ (2 Kings 25:13).
passages.asks: Every piece was made with care, by name and by measure, for the worship of God. Ask what care you give to the ordinary things that serve worship where you are. And ask what you would grieve if it were broken up and carried off.
